newsitem.title: USA: Health groups reject key terms of tobacco pact.
newsitem.headline: Health groups reject key terms of tobacco pact.

text.p: Public health advocates Wednesday rejected a key part of the proposed tobacco settlement, calling any constraints on the Food and Drug Administration's ability to regulate nicotine "absolutely unacceptable."

They also demanded that tobacco companies face "predictable and severe" financial sanctions if they fail to meet goals for cutting youth smoking. The agreement currently sets out an $80 million fine for each percentage point off the target, which translates to about five cents per cigarette pack sold.

The recommendations of the nation's leading public health organisations are not binding but are expected to carry great weight as Congress considers legislation needed to enact the settlement reached by industry and state officials last week, which calls for cigarette makers to pay $368.5 billion and submit to federal regulation.

The advisory council, comprising major medical and health groups as well anti-smoking organisations, was formed at the behest of some anti-tobacco lawmakers and is headed by former FDA commissioner David Kessler and former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop.

The council has not taken a stand on whether they would prefer trying to improve the proposed settlement between the tobacco companies and the 40 states suing them, or whether they believe it is too weak and cannot be salvaged.
Kessler said he does not plan to push for a consensus on that, although both he and Koop favour trying to improve the settlement package.

But the health groups' position regarding FDA oversight was striking after a split had emerged in recent weeks. Several groups that had endorsed the general thrust of the settlement talks, including the American Heart Association, the American Medical Association (AMA) and the American Cancer Society, said they could not accept the FDA language in the proposal.
"The FDA is the core of it all," Randolph Smoak, secretary-treasurer of the AMA, told Reuters. "It has to be tied down so there is no wiggle room or loopholes for the industry."

The agreement between the cigarette companies and the state attorneys general suing them recognised FDA authority but set conditions that the health advocates argued would effectively allow the tobacco industry to fend off regulation.

"The FDA should continue to have immediate and explicit authority to regulate all areas of nicotine" and other ingredients of tobacco products, the health organisations said, noting that after a long battle a federal court recently upheld FDA jurisdiction over tobacco.
Even Bill Novelli, a representative of the Campaign for Tobacco Free Kids, which helped negotiate the deal, concurred that getting full recognition for the FDA authority was "non-negotiable."
But he cautioned other panel members to be realistic about other aspects of the accord, and not be too hasty about rejecting its public health components.
Both Kessler and Koop said they would prefer to see a settlement, although both consider the current agreement as deeply and unacceptably flawed.
"Personally, I would like to see a resolution -- but not in the words of this settlement," Kessler said.
"It has to be fixed, it can be fixed, and we will fix it," said Koop, adding he was concerned whether "Congress will go along."
Congressional Republican leaders have not commented on the substance of the pact and have said Congress will have to study it at length before taking action.

The Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled three hearings over the next month to review the agreement but not weigh specific legislation to enact it. Witnesses for the first hearing set for Thursday all took part in the settlement talks. The White House has said it will set up a task force to
study the settlement proposal. Touching on health, taxes, product liability and possibly farming and foreign trade, any legislation to enact it would be extremely complex.
